newsitem.title: GERMANY: Porsche says may consider Europe, U.S. plant sites.
newsitem.headline: Porsche says may consider Europe, U.S. plant sites.

text.p: The chief executive of German luxury carmaker Porsche AG said on Saturday he saw good chances to build another production location in Europe but also possibly in the United States.

Porsche chief executive Wendelin Wiedking also told Germany's Welt am Sonntag newspaper that the Stuttgart-based carmaker would be forced to reduce its temporary workforce in Germany in order to secure the long-term jobs of its workforce.

"The United States is the largest export market for us and the acceptance by Americans to buy products made in their country is very large," Wiedeking said in discussing whether Porsche may consider America for a new production plant.

Porsche has seen strong demand for its Boxster roadster, which was first introduced last autumn, and signed a deal with Finland's Valmet Oy to assemble some of the Boxsters after Porsche decided not to expand German-based production.
Porsche's Stuttgart plant, which has a capacity of about 30,000 cars a year, cannot keep up with demand which now has an order backlog of about a year.
He reaffirmed no German company had fulfilled the criteria to assemble the Boxsters, a move that would have helped to create jobs in Germany at a time of near-record unemployment.
Wiedeking also said Porsche, which has cut about 2,500 jobs in recent years, was seeking to reduce the number of temporary worker contracts.

"We will not be able to keep on these workers in a longer time frame," he said, noting only the main workers could be guaranteed job security," Wiedeking said, noting gains in productivity have cut the time need to build Porsche cars.
He said the carmaker may also consider dropping out of national employer associations and negotiating directly with unions in a bid to improve its competitive stance.

In addition, Wiedeking said Porsche was still very interested in building a sport utility vehicle after partnership talks with Mercedes-Benz AG broke down in early 1997, saying Porsche may opt to build the car alone.
